classification.tone: Gritty, oppressive, tragic, and increasingly nightmarish

evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving miniature artist discovers her family’s dead daughter may be channeling something ancient and malevolent — and the truth turns the house into a trap.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has immediate genre pull: grief, family collapse, and escalating supernatural dread all land in a clean commercial lane. The funeral, the seance, the school breakdown, and the final treehouse revelation give it the kind of word-of-mouth horror engine that travels well.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook arrives early and keeps sharpening: a mother’s grief, a son’s panic, a daughter’s strange behavior, and a hidden occult design all become legible fast. The miniature motif and the family-home setting give the story a distinct engine that is easy to explain in one breath.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Annie is a loaded lead role built on contradiction — artist, mother, mourner, skeptic, believer — and Peter’s collapse gives the film a second emotional center. Steve and Charlie deepen the family system, and the roles all have actor-facing material that can carry the movie beyond the plot mechanics.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a rare blend of domestic realism, occult ritual, and miniature-as-fate imagery, and it does so with confidence. The visual grammar of dollhouse, diorama, and overhead composition gives the film its own signature language.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps tightening the vise: funeral to school incident to seance to possession to revelation to final takeover. Each major sequence escalates the family’s inability to explain what’s happening, and the ending lands as a full-throttle payoff.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels both strange and inevitable: a family grief drama that gradually reveals itself as a ritual possession story. The emotional logic and the occult logic lock together so cleanly that the film’s final turn feels earned rather than ornamental.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is rich with tactile detail — the workshop, the support group, the school, the funeral home, the attic, the treehouse, the ritual materials. Those spaces are not just backdrops; they keep generating story and visual meaning.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakable: intimate family drama colliding with escalating supernatural horror, played with a cold, controlled seriousness that makes the shocks hit harder. The film can move from awkward dinner-table realism to full possession spectacle without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The surface story is a haunting, but underneath it sits a much larger design about inheritance, control, motherhood, and identity. The miniature house, the family history, and the occult lineage all suggest a deeper mythology that rewards a second look.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Graham family is a strong relational engine: Annie/Steve, Annie/Peter, Steve/Peter, Annie/Charlie, and the absent-but-haunting Ellen all generate tension. Even Joan functions as a destabilizing relational force, which gives the film multiple pressure points instead of a single lead-only track.

casting_characteristics: One child/teen role with special-needs classroom context
One older supporting female role with strong occult presence
One family ensemble centered on mother, father, son, daughter

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with some exterior night/day sequences
notable_requirements: Family house with attic and treehouse
Funeral home chapel and viewing room
High school classroom, gym, hallway, and party house

technical.vfx_details: Supernatural manifestations, floating/ceiling movement, possession effects, ant swarms, fire transitions, and miniature-to-real visual transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical fire effects, decapitation aftermath, corpse makeup, flies, ants, blood, and practical possession beats.

rights_flags.detail: Serafem and Lexapro are named in Steve’s psychiatry office dialogue.
Facebook is shown on Peter’s laptop.
M&Ms are visible in Charlie’s bedroom scene.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Prestige theatrical horror / premium streamer horror
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform or specialty theatrical runway

cost.note: The house, workshop, school, and apartment footprint keep the spend grounded, but the possession effects, fire work, corpse work, and ant/fly imagery push above a low-budget lane.

cast.note: The film is anchored by a family quartet plus a key supporting occult figure, and the child/teen casting needs are specific enough to shape the package.

location.note: The story is mostly contained, but it moves through a meaningful spread of interiors and a few night exteriors, including the woods, highway, and school spaces.

content.note: Grief, child death, decapitation, possession, self-harm imagery, and body horror make this firmly adult-facing.

rights.note: The script uses a few generic brands and medication names, but there is no major IP or life-rights dependency.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The miniature motif is the film’s signature.
strengths.what_it_means: The dollhouse and model-work give the movie a visual identity that can be marketed instantly and remembered long after the plot details fade. Horror buyers and prestige genre audiences alike respond to a concept that has both iconography and thematic function.
strengths.evidence: Annie’s workshop, the replicated Graham house, and the repeated push-ins from full-scale space into miniature space.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Annie is a showcase lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part gives an actress grief, rage, denial, dark humor, and supernatural escalation in one performance, which is exactly the kind of role that can anchor a prestige horror campaign. Festival programmers, awards-minded buyers, and actors looking for a career-defining turn will all see the value immediately.
strengths.evidence: The funeral eulogy, the support-group confession, the workshop breakdown, and the seance sequence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family dynamic keeps generating pressure.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not a one-note haunted-house setup; the marriage, parent-child bonds, and sibling tension all create separate engines that keep the film alive scene after scene. That makes the project attractive to buyers who want horror with acting meat and emotional replay value.
strengths.evidence: The dinner-table blowup, Steve’s professional distance, Peter’s guilt, and Annie’s fixation on Charlie.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The occult reveal is earned, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: The script starts as grief drama and gradually reveals a hidden ritual architecture, which gives the ending a sense of inevitability instead of gimmick. That kind of structural turn is catnip for genre audiences because it rewards attention and invites rewatching.
strengths.evidence: Joan’s seance, the sigil, the books in the attic, and the final Paimon revelation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The film has a clean prestige-horror lane.
strengths.what_it_means: It sits in the sweet spot where elevated character work and full-bodied horror can coexist, which broadens the buyer conversation beyond pure genre. That makes it attractive to specialty theatrical distributors, premium streamers, and producers looking for a breakout horror title with awards-adjacent craft.
strengths.evidence: The support group scene, the psychiatrist husband, the funeral-home setting, and the final supernatural set pieces.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The house itself becomes a story engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Because the home, attic, workshop, and treehouse all carry narrative meaning, the production can keep returning to a finite set of spaces while still feeling expansive. Buyers like contained worlds that still feel rich enough to support escalating dread and strong trailer moments.
strengths.evidence: The Graham house, the attic hatch, the workshop miniatures, and the treehouse finale.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige horror package with a real identity: a grief-soaked family collapse told through one of the most memorable visual motifs in recent genre writing. It gives a lead actress a monster role, gives the film a marketable iconography, and builds to a finale that feels both shocking and inevitable.

lead_characters.name: Annie Graham
lead_characters.hook: Annie is a tightly wound miniature artist whose need to control form is really a need to control grief, memory, and family chaos. She is funny, brittle, defensive, and emotionally ferocious, with a mind that keeps trying to rationalize what her body and home are refusing to explain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in *Hereditary* itself: a role where breakdown is not a single scene but the engine of the entire film. Actors who want a prestige horror centerpiece — the kind that lets them play maternal love, humiliation, fury, and possession in one arc — will chase this immediately.

lead_characters.name: Steve Graham
lead_characters.hook: Steve is the family’s stabilizer, a polished psychiatrist who believes in procedure, language, and emotional containment right up until the house stops obeying reason. He is loving but paternalistic, calm until cornered, and increasingly trapped between professional skepticism and private terror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of a grounded prestige husband role like Gabriel Byrne in *In Treatment* or *Miller’s Crossing* — a man whose composure becomes the thing the audience watches crack. Character actors who can play authority, fatigue, and moral helplessness will see a rich, adult part here.

lead_characters.name: Peter Graham
lead_characters.hook: Peter is a disengaged, awkward teenager who drifts through the story in a haze of guilt, desire, and self-protection until the supernatural starts using his body as a battleground. He reads as emotionally underpowered at first, which becomes the point: he is a boy whose passivity curdles into panic and then into something far stranger.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Alex Wolff gets in *The Cat and the Moon* or *Hereditary* — a teen/young adult part that turns anxiety into a full-body performance. Young actors looking for a terrifying, emotionally exposed showcase will want this because it asks for fear, shame, dissociation, and physical collapse.

lead_characters.name: Charlie Graham
lead_characters.hook: Charlie is an eerie, self-contained teenager with a deadpan presence, a clicking tic, and an artist’s eye that makes her feel both childlike and ancient. She is socially alien, visually distinctive, and emotionally unreadable in a way that makes every gesture feel loaded.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that made Milly Shapiro unforgettable in *Hereditary* — a role where stillness, physical specificity, and unsettling presence do the heavy lifting. Young performers with unusual screen presence and casting directors looking for a truly singular face will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.hook: Joan presents as a warm grief ally and then reveals herself as the film’s most quietly dangerous human conduit. She is maternal, welcoming, and spiritually persuasive, which makes her far more unsettling than a conventional villain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Ann Dowd has made a specialty of in *The Leftovers* and *Mass* — a character who can be tender, unnerving, and spiritually absolute in the same breath. Veteran character actresses who can turn kindness into menace will want this part.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Mason
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Mason is the outside professional authority brought in to restore order, but he arrives too late to contain what the family has already set in motion. He functions as the rational witness who can still be shaken by the scale of the collapse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained authority role that lets an actor play calm expertise under pressure, similar to the grounded professional energy in *Ordinary People* or *The Father*. Strong supporting players who specialize in credibility and emotional restraint will be interested.

lead_characters.name: Bridget
lead_characters.hook: Bridget is the cool, slightly detached teen girl who becomes Peter’s object of longing and a brief reminder of ordinary adolescent life. She is not a plot engine so much as a pressure point for Peter’s embarrassment and desire.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but useful teen role in the lane of the socially observant girls in *Lady Bird* — a part that benefits from naturalism and a sharp sense of timing. Young actors with indie credibility or rising TV visibility would see it as an easy fit.

lead_characters.name: Brendan
lead_characters.hook: Brendan is one of Peter’s stoner friends, a casual teenage presence who helps expose Peter’s social drift and panic. He is comic texture, but he also helps make Peter’s isolation feel real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of teen supporting role that gives a young actor a few memorable beats without carrying the movie, similar to the friend roles in *Superbad* or *Eighth Grade*. It’s a clean fit for emerging talent who can play natural, loose, and slightly obnoxious.

lead_characters.name: Mr. Davies
lead_characters.hook: Mr. Davies is the classroom adult who tries to make meaning out of tragedy through literature, only to watch Peter unravel in real time. He is patient, observant, and increasingly alarmed by what he cannot reach.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong teacher role in the lane of the humane adult figures in *Dead Poets Society* or *The Holdovers* — a part that gets to be smart, sympathetic, and briefly helpless. Character actors who can play warmth without sentimentality will like it.

lead_characters.name: Teacher
lead_characters.hook: Charlie’s teacher is a gentle classroom authority who treats her with care and patience. He exists as one of the few adults who seems to understand Charlie’s difference without trying to correct it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but actor-friendly role for someone who can make a few lines feel lived-in and humane, like the understated school-adult parts in *The Florida Project*. It’s a clean supporting slot for a recognizable character actor.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make domestic horror feel operatic without losing realism.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with one or two features, or elevated-genre filmmakers coming out of festival shorts and character-driven work. The sweet spot is someone who cares about visual symbolism, performance pressure, and controlled escalation more than jump-scare mechanics.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards precision in blocking, framing, and tonal control because the miniature imagery and family scenes have to feel emotionally true before the horror lands. It attracts directors who want a signature horror film that still plays like serious drama.

buyer_appeal.lane: Prestige horror / specialty theatrical / premium streamer genre
buyer_appeal.detail: The Annie role can justify a name-talent anchor, but the contained house-and-family footprint means the movie can still be packaged around performance and a strong director reel. The grief-plus-occult lane has durable streamer demand and a specialty theatrical path when the marketing can lean on iconography and critical buzz.

considerations.area: The family history can be foregrounded earlier.
considerations.detail: The script’s occult reveal lands hard because the emotional groundwork is strong; one next-pass lever would be to seed a little more of Ellen’s spiritualism and Joan’s connection before the attic discovery. That would make the final lineage reveal feel even more inevitable while preserving the mystery.

considerations.area: The support-group material carries the exposition load.
considerations.detail: The long confession scene is powerful, but it also does a lot of backstory lifting in one stretch. A version that lets one or two of those facts surface in earlier, smaller exchanges would keep the emotional force while smoothing the information flow.

considerations.area: The occult mechanics are dense by design.
considerations.detail: The Paimon material, the sigils, the books, and the ritual language all create a rich mythology, but they also ask the audience to track a lot of symbolic information late in the film. A simplification pass that preserves the same ritual logic with fewer named elements could make the final act even cleaner for a broad audience.

considerations.area: The production footprint is contained but effect-heavy.
considerations.detail: The house, workshop, school, and apartment structure keeps the location count manageable, while the possession, fire, corpse, and insect work drive the spectacle. The cleanest production path is to protect the contained footprint and concentrate resources on the handful of set pieces that define the movie.

considerations.area: The child-actor material needs careful casting.
considerations.detail: Charlie and Peter both carry major emotional and physical load, and Charlie’s stillness plus Peter’s panic have to read with precision. The right young performers will do a lot of the movie’s heavy lifting, so casting chemistry is a major packaging lever.
